So the lesson for web developers is in the short term if your server doesn't use global rate limits you don't need to worry at this time.

In the long term, use https, write your app in a way where you assume any byte combination could come from any ip as seen by your server even one of your legitamite users with that ip isn't actually the one sending it. Sessions + https + verifying authorization to do anything that writes to db.

And also assume that if you aren't using https that your users can recieve any content even if you didn't send it, including sign-in forms. This is an off the path attack so they the attacker doesn't get to see the original request so a sign-in form would be odd being served for h-ttp://somedomain/staticarticlethatdoesntneedsignin, but also off the path it could be attempted from anywhere in the world so spray and pray could be attempted.

Basically at the tcp level you are getting a socket per user on your site. How does it know messages sent from user A is meant for their socket, an identifier. So someone can inject on their socket.

This is probably worse for SMTP which is often unencrypted and stateful. Stateful meaning a socket establishment is a signin rather than a cookie being sent with each smtp command.
